title: Disney+ and Hulu Hike Prices Up to 13% After Doubling Profits, Says Ars Technica
body:
Disney announced a second‑round price hike for its streaming services this month, lifting the cost of both Disney+ and Hulu by as much as 13 percent. The increases come on the heels of a quarterly report that showed Disney’s direct‑to‑consumer division more than doubled its profit year over year, prompting executives to argue that the higher fees are needed to sustain the company’s expanding content slate and to fund its increasingly sophisticated ad‑free offerings. For many subscribers, however, the new rates place Disney+’s premium tier above the price of Netflix’s most popular plan, intensifying competition in a market where price sensitivity is becoming a decisive factor.

The ad‑free Disney+ tier, which previously cost $7.99 per month in the United States, now climbs to $9.99, while the bundled Disney+, Hulu (ad‑free) and ESPN+ package rises from $13.99 to $15.99. Hulu’s standalone ad‑free plan also sees a $1 increase, moving to $7.99. Internationally, Disney+ subscribers in Canada, the United Kingdom and other regions will see comparable adjustments, generally ranging between 10 and 13 percent. The company says the hikes will support “continued investment in original storytelling, technology, and a broader global footprint.” 

Analysts note that Disney’s decision reflects both confidence and caution. The streaming unit posted a net profit of $1.4 billion for the quarter, up from $630 million a year earlier, driven largely by subscriber growth in emerging markets and a surge in ad‑supported revenue. Yet the same earnings call highlighted rising content costs, with Disney allocating roughly $15 billion annually to produce movies, series, and specials for its platforms. The price increase, therefore, is positioned as a means to offset those expenses without compromising the breadth of its library, which now includes high‑budget franchises like “The Mandalorian,” “Marvel Studios” releases, and the revived “National Geographic” documentaries.

The move also underscores a broader industry trend: streaming services are shifting from aggressive subscriber acquisition to monetization of an increasingly mature user base. Netflix, which raised its standard plan to $15.49 earlier this year, has already signaled that price elasticity is manageable for its core audience. Disney’s ad‑free tier now surpasses Netflix’s “Standard” plan, which offers two simultaneous streams at $15.49, while Disney+ still limits ad‑free viewing to a single screen. This pricing parity could push price‑conscious households to reconsider which platform offers the best value, especially as competitors like HBO Max and Peacock continue to experiment with tiered, ad‑supported models.

Consumer reaction has been mixed. Some longtime Disney fans expressed disappointment, citing the brand’s reputation for family‑friendly pricing and the perception that the service’s value proposition has eroded as more exclusive content migrates to theatrical releases or other Disney‑owned platforms. Others argue that the higher fee is justified by the premium quality of Disney’s original programming and the convenience of a consolidated bundle that includes sports and general‑interest streaming. Social media chatter reflects both frustration over “price gouging” and acceptance that “the cost of great content is rising across the board.”

Looking ahead, Disney’s pricing strategy may set the tone for the next phase of the streaming wars. If the company can retain its subscriber base while maintaining profit margins, it may embolden other players to follow suit, potentially leading to a tiered market where ad‑free experiences become a premium offering. Conversely, sustained subscriber churn could force Disney to recalibrate its approach, perhaps by expanding its ad‑supported tier or introducing more flexible, à la carte options. For now, the price hike signals Disney’s confidence in its content arsenal and its willingness to leverage profitability to fund future growth, while the ultimate test will be whether viewers deem the added cost worth the magic on their screens.
